blocks.text: 9.1.3. Builder Pattern

A customer is refunded 45.00 EUR for order 7781. The next morning reconciliation finds the shop's account 45.00 richer and the customer's 45.00 poorer. The refund code compiled, its tests passed, and every field of the transfer it created held a valid value. Two arguments were in the wrong order.
A builder is for objects like that one: many parts, several of the same type, some optional. Every output below is from Java 21.
Same-Typed Constructor Arguments Swap Without an Error; a Builder Names Each One
The transfer class grew one constructor per optional part, the telescoping style:
Before reading the output, decide which balance goes up:

Transfer[from=ACC-2002 (customer), to=ACC-1001 (shop), cents=4500, currency=EUR, memo=refund order 7781]
{ACC-1001 (shop)=54500, ACC-2002 (customer)=-4500}

`customer` and `shop` are both `String`, so the swapped call matches the constructor exactly. The compiler checks types. A test that builds a transfer from its own literals and reads them back passes in either order. Nothing fails until the money is in the wrong account.
The telescope has a second cost. A memo without a currency would need `Transfer(String, String, long, String memo)`, and that signature is taken:
clash/Transfer.java:25: error: constructor Transfer(String,String,long,String) is already defined in class Transfer

So a caller who wants a memo passes every value before it, which is how a five-argument call with adjacent `String`s comes about. Here is the same class with a builder: a private constructor that takes the builder, and one method per part.

Transfer refund = Transfer.builder()
        .from(shop)
        .to(customer)
        .cents(4_500)
        .memo("refund order 7781")
        .build();

Transfer[from=ACC-1001 (shop), to=ACC-2002 (customer), cents=4500, currency=EUR, memo=refund order 7781]
{ACC-1001 (shop)=45500, ACC-2002 (customer)=4500}

The caller set a memo without passing a currency, which took its default. The builder doesn't make the compiler reject `.from(customer)`; it puts the word `from` next to the value, where a reviewer reads it. Only distinct types, such as a `PayerAccount` and a `PayeeAccount`, turn the swap into a compile error. A record's canonical constructor is positional too (unit 2.4.3 shows the same swap), and a static factory (unit 9.1.2) names one way to create an object, not each part.
A Builder Checks the Whole Object in build(), Where Every Part Is Set
A transfer to its own account is a mistake, and someone adds the check to the `to()` setter so it fails as early as possible:
Three callers: two orders, and one forgotten part. `attempt` prints the transfer, or the exception.

from, then to: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: transfer to its own account ACC-1001
to, then from: Transfer[from=ACC-1001, to=ACC-1001, cents=4500, currency=EUR, memo=]
no to:         Transfer[from=ACC-1001, to=null, cents=4500, currency=EUR, memo=]

When `to()` runs first, `fromAccount` is still `null`, and the check compares against nothing. A setter sees one part. A rule that relates two parts, or requires one, belongs in `build()`, the call that says the caller is done. The same checks, moved there:

from, then to: java.lang.IllegalStateException: transfer to its own account ACC-1001
to, then from: java.lang.IllegalStateException: transfer to its own account ACC-1001
no to:         java.lang.IllegalStateException: from and to are required

The product's constructor is private and only `build()` calls it, so no path to a `Transfer` skips the checks. A setter may still reject a value that is wrong on its own, such as a negative amount, at once.

For a type with three required parts, a builder is more code than it saves. A record's compact constructor runs its checks on every path to an instance, including a `with` method that calls `new` (unit 2.4.1):
With `monthly = new Fee("ACC-1001", 990, "EUR")`, `monthly.withCents(1_490)`, then `monthly.withCents(0)`:

Fee[account=ACC-1001, cents=1490, currency=EUR]
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: cents must be positive: 0
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Builder Used Again After build() Changes What It Built, Unless the Product Copies

Transfers now carry tags, which reconciliation matches on. The monthly payroll run sets the payer and a batch tag once, then reuses the builder for each employee. The builder collects tags in a list, and `Transfer` gets a `tags()` accessor:

private final List<String> tags = new ArrayList<>();      // in Transfer.Builder

public Builder tag(String tag) { this.tags.add(tag); return this; }
We ran it three times, each with another version of the line in `Transfer`'s constructor that keeps the tags, labelled in the output:

this.tags = b.tags;                                   // shared
this.tags = Collections.unmodifiableList(b.tags);     // view
this.tags = List.copyOf(b.tags);                      // copy

shared:
first, when built:     [payroll-2026-10, E-17]
first, after second:   [payroll-2026-10, E-17, E-18]
second:                [payroll-2026-10, E-17, E-18]
view:
first, when built:     [payroll-2026-10, E-17]
first, after second:   [payroll-2026-10, E-17, E-18]
second:                [payroll-2026-10, E-17, E-18]
copy:
first, when built:     [payroll-2026-10, E-17]
first, after second:   [payroll-2026-10, E-17]
second:                [payroll-2026-10, E-17, E-18]

With the first two, the transfer to employee 17, built and perhaps already sent, changed when the builder was used for employee 18, and reconciliation now matches it to both. The builder's list keeps changing while the builder is used, and a product that holds a reference to it changes with it. `Collections.unmodifiableList` stops the product's readers from writing, but it is a view of the same list, so the builder's writes still show through. `List.copyOf` takes an unmodifiable copy of the builder's `ArrayList`. Unit 2.4.2 shows the same leak through a record's list component.

The copy fixes the first transfer, and the second still carries `E-17`, because the builder keeps every tag it was given. To use a builder as a template, give it a `copy()` method and build each product from a copy, or create a new builder per product. A builder kept in a static field, a singleton in the sense of unit 9.1.1, is reused by every thread that calls it.
<!-- practice 2 -->
HttpRequest.Builder Copies on build(), but a Reused Builder Keeps Adding Headers

`java.net.http.HttpRequest` is created through `HttpRequest.newBuilder()`, and building a request sends nothing, so it runs without a network. A payout client reuses one builder for two payouts, each with its own idempotency key:
The same two payouts, each built from `copy()` of `template`, a builder set up exactly like `payouts`:
The keys of each pair, then the method, URI, timeout and body length of request `b`:

reused:  first [po-17], second [po-17, po-18]
copy():  first [po-17], second [po-18]
POST https://api.example.com/v1/payouts PT5S 16 bytes

The first request still has one key after the second was built: `build()` copies the builder's state into an immutable request, the fix of the previous section. The second request has two, because `header()` adds a value, and which one the payout API reads is up to that API. `setHeader()` replaces the value, but it still changes the shared builder. `copy()` returns a new builder with the template's state, and nothing done to the copy reaches the template.
The JDK's builder checks a part in its setter when the part alone can be wrong, and leaves only the missing URI to `build()`. Each of these four ran on its own, and only the first calls `build()`:

() -> HttpRequest.newBuilder().header("Accept", "application/json").build(),
() -> HttpRequest.newBuilder().uri(URI.create("ftp://files.example.com/payouts.csv")),
() -> HttpRequest.newBuilder().header("Content-Length", "10"),
() -> HttpRequest.newBuilder().timeout(Duration.ZERO)

java.lang.IllegalStateException: uri is null
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: invalid URI scheme ftp
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: restricted header name: "Content-Length"
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Invalid duration: PT0S
`StringBuilder` is a growing character buffer with nothing to validate, despite the name (unit 1.4.5).

Summary

items: **Same-typed constructor arguments swap without an error.** A builder names each part at the call site and lets optional parts take defaults; only distinct types make a swap fail to compile.

**A builder checks the whole object in `build()`.** A setter that checks one part against another depends on call order, and a missing part gets through as `null`. For a small type, a record's compact constructor does the same job.

**A builder used again after `build()` changes what it built, unless the product copies.** A read-only view still shows the builder's writes; `List.copyOf` doesn't. Reuse also carries every earlier part into the next product.
**`HttpRequest.Builder` copies on `build()`, and `header()` adds.** Start each request from `copy()` of a template.

blocks.text: Reference
**`HttpRequest.Builder` (Java 21):**

rows: a scheme other than `http` or `https`, or no host, at the call (`IllegalArgumentException`)
a restricted name such as `Content-Length`, an invalid name or value, at the call (`IllegalArgumentException`)
zero or negative, at the call (`IllegalArgumentException`)
nothing; returns a new builder with the same state

blocks.text: `header(name, value)` adds a value to the name; `setHeader(name, value)` replaces its values.
**Keeping a builder's list in the product:**

rows: yes, if the getter returns it

blocks.text: Challenges

items: Your `Order` has nine parts, four of them required. Compare a builder that takes the required ones in its constructor with one that checks them in `build()`. Which mistakes does each catch, and when?
Sketch a builder whose `build()` can only be called after `from()` and `to()`, so the compiler rejects a missing part. What does each added required part cost?
Find a builder in your codebase that is reused in a loop. Write the test that fails if the second product carries a part of the first.

blocks.text: Design Note: Why Java Has Builders and Not Named Arguments

Languages with named and default arguments let the caller name each argument and leave out the optional ones, which covers most of what builders and telescoping constructors are for. Java has neither, so the builder supplies both, at the price of a second class that mirrors the product's fields and must be kept in step with it: add a field to `Transfer` and forget the builder method, and nothing can set it. The GoF form adds a director that drives one sequence of steps over different builders to produce different representations. It is rare in Java code.
